newsitem.title: UK: UK's Major pitches for small business vote.
newsitem.headline: UK's Major pitches for small business vote.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major pitched on Tuesday for the votes of Britain's growing army of small businessmen by proposing an 800 million pound tax break for fledgling firms.

Major travelled to the central city of Birmingham, the workshop of Britain, to unveil the plan, which was designed to overshadow the much-heralded launch due on Friday of the main Labour opposition party's small business manifesto.

The prime minister, whose party is running 20 points behind in the race for the May 1 election, was scathing about opposition leader Tony Blair's claim that Labour had become the natural party of small business.
Denouncing what he called the "stunt-a-day opposition", Major said Labour's conversion to free-market policies was as fantastical as anything in Alice in Wonderland.
"I sometimes believe that this modern Labour party, if it had a collective grandmother, would sell it," Major told a lunch for Asian small businessmen at Edgbaston cricket ground.

Earlier, he told a news conference there were now one million more small firms in Britain than in 1979, when the Conservatives took office, making a total of 3.5 million. Together, they employed 10 million people.
"Whereas Labour made big businesses small, we've helped small businesses grow big," he said. "Soon they'll employ more than half the workforce. They are today's sign of tomorrow's economic health."
To give them an extra hand-up, Major said the Conservatives would reform the system of local business taxes by giving each firm a 1,000-pound ($1,623) allowance.
This would have the effect of redistributing the tax burden from small firms to bigger companies that can more easily bear it.

More than 750,000 companies would benefit from a reduction in the so-called Universal Business Rate, representing 90 percent of all firms with annual turnover of less than 100,000 pounds, and 140,000 companies would escape the local tax net altogether, he explained.
Major, who was scarred as a young man by the failure of his father's garden ornament business, said small businesses had been a big influence in his life.
"For small firms the choice at this election is clear," he wrote in the foreword to his party's small business manifesto, published on Tuesday.

"It is between the Conservative Party that has aided their success and will continue to meet their needs in future, and a Labour party that has fought all our reforms and would burden them with higher taxes, more regulation and trade union powers," he wrote.
